args.body:
DEVIATION REPORT
Cross-Border Data Transfer Agreement
Counterparty Markup Analysis
Data Privacy & Cybersecurity

CONFIDENTIAL — ATTORNEY WORK PRODUCT
Prepared for: Deal Team
Re: Analysis of Counterparty Markup Against Original Draft, Playbook, Transfer Impact Summary, and Partner Instructions

---

I. PURPOSE AND SCOPE

This deviation report reconciles the counterparty's markup of the Cross-Border Data Transfer Agreement against (i) our original draft and firm-standard playbook positions, (ii) the transfer impact summary (disclosure schedules and exhibits), and (iii) the controlling partner instructions circulated on this engagement. The report identifies each deviation introduced by the counterparty, assesses its impact in light of the disclosed schedules, and recommends a position consistent with the partner's controlling priorities. The misfiled administrative correspondence in this matter folder was excluded from consideration, as it concerns an unrelated engagement.

The engagement instruction directed counsel to compare the counterparty markup against the original draft and playbook, incorporating the transfer impact summary and partner instructions, and to produce a full deviation report (deviation-report.docx). The controlling partner correspondence states that the client will concede the basket conversion but treats any survival-period reduction as a walk-away issue. Only the latest message controls; earlier superseded instructions stating the opposite ordering are disregarded.

---

II. SUMMARY OF DEVIATIONS IDENTIFIED

The counterparty's markup accepted most firm-standard provisions but introduced the following three deviations:

1. Indemnification Cap Reduction and Basket Conversion
2. Material Adverse Effect (MAE) Definition Carve-Outs for Regulatory Action
3. Limitation Period Shortening Survival for Core Representations

Each deviation is analyzed below against the base materials, the transfer impact summary (Schedules and Exhibits), and the controlling partner instructions.

---

III. DEVIATION 1 — INDEMNIFICATION CAP REDUCTION AND BASKET CONVERSION

A. What the Counterparty Proposed

The counterparty's markup silently reduces the indemnification cap and converts the basket from a deductible to a tipping basket. Under the original draft and firm-standard playbook, the indemnification cap is set at the negotiated limit and the basket operates as a deductible, such that the indemnified party bears all loss once the basket threshold is reached. In a tipping basket regime, the counterparty becomes liable for all losses above the threshold—typically a more favorable structure for the indemnified party than a deductible.

B. Transfer Impact — Schedule 5.2

Schedule 5.2 of the disclosure schedules lists retained liabilities that the counterparty's indemnification changes would silently shift. The scheduled exceptions identify liabilities that remain with the relevant party and that the indemnification provisions, as drafted in our original agreement, would not transfer. The counterparty's simultaneous reduction of the cap and conversion of the basket structure must be assessed against the scope of these retained liabilities. If the tip/basket conversion is combined with a cap reduction, the net effect is ambiguous: the tipping basket marginally benefits the indemnified party while the cap reduction erodes the overall recovery available. The interplay between the two changes creates a net position that requires quantification against the Schedule 5.2 retained liabilities.

C. Partner Instruction — Controlling Position

The latest partner instruction directs that the client will concede the basket conversion. This is the controlling instruction. However, while the client is willing to accept the conversion of the basket from a deductible to a tipping mechanism, the accompanying silent reduction of the indemnification cap is a separate and distinct deviation that remains open. The partner has not authorized concession of the cap reduction. The cap reduction must therefore be treated as a contested item.

D. Recommendation

• Accept the basket conversion (deductible → tipping) consistent with the controlling partner instruction.
• Reject the silent reduction of the indemnification cap. The cap should remain at the level set in the original draft absent further partner authorization. Counterparty should be required to justify any cap reduction in light of the Schedule 5.2 retained liabilities.
• Ensure that any final indemnification structure preserves the allocation of retained liabilities reflected in Schedule 5.2, which the counterparty's combined markup changes would otherwise silently shift.

---

IV. DEVIATION 2 — MATERIAL ADVERSE EFFECT (MAE) DEFINITION CARVE-OUTS FOR REGULATORY ACTION

A. What the Counterparty Proposed

The counterparty's markup adds carve-outs to the definition of Material Adverse Effect for regulatory action "of exactly the kind at issue in this matter." If accepted, these carve-outs would exclude specified regulatory developments from the scope of what constitutes an MAE, thereby limiting the circumstances that could trigger an MAE determination.

B. Transfer Impact — Schedule 3.7

Schedule 3.7 discloses two pending regulatory inquiries that intersect the counterparty's proposed MAE carve-outs. The scheduled exceptions confirm that two regulatory proceedings are already underway and known to the parties. The counterparty's attempt to carve out regulatory action from the MAE definition is directly targeted at these disclosed inquiries. Acceptance of the carve-outs would effectively remove the operational risk posed by the two pending regulatory proceedings from the MAE framework entirely—meaning that adverse developments in those inquiries would not constitute an MAE and would not support the remedies available under the agreement. This is a material adverse shift to the client's protections.

C. Interaction with Base Materials

The playbook and original draft treat MAE carve-outs narrowly, reserving broad MAE protection. The counterparty's proposed regulatory-action carve-out is not a standard-market carve-out of the type typically included (e.g., general economic or industry-wide conditions). Instead, it is a targeted carve-out designed to insulate the counterparty from the specific regulatory risk already disclosed on Schedule 3.7. The scheduled exceptions control over any general statements in the base materials, and Schedule 3.7's disclosure of the two pending inquiries confirms that this carve-out is purpose-built rather than a market-standard proviso.

D. Recommendation

• Reject the proposed regulatory-action carve-outs to the MAE definition, because they are specifically designed to neutralize the two pending regulatory inquiries already disclosed on Schedule 3.7.
• If the counterparty insists on some regulatory carve-out, narrow any such carve-out to exclude matters already disclosed on Schedule 3.7 or to require an exception only for regulatory developments outside the scope of the disclosed inquiries, consistent with the playbook's narrow MAE carve-out approach.
• Flag this deviation as a substantive risk-allocation shift requiring escalation, given that it directly undermines the protections tied to known regulatory exposure.

---

V. DEVIATION 3 — LIMITATION PERIOD SHORTENING SURVIVAL FOR CORE REPRESENTATIONS

A. What the Counterparty Proposed

The counterparty's markup introduces a new limitation period that shortens the survival of the core representations. This is a substantive reduction from the survival periods reflected in the original draft and firm-standard playbook.

B. Transfer Impact — Exhibit B

Exhibit B of the disclosure schedules sets the survival matrix that governs how long representations, warranties, and covenants survive closing and remain actionable. The counterparty's proposed limitation-period change directly contradicts the survival matrix set forth in Exhibit B. The scheduled exceptions and Exhibit B control over any general statements in the base materials. Accordingly, the survival periods in Exhibit B represent the operative baseline against which the counterparty's shortening must be measured. The counterparty's proposal would materially truncate the window during which the client could pursue claims for breach of the core representations.

C. Partner Instruction — Walk-Away Issue

The controlling partner instruction states that the client treats any survival-period reduction as a walk-away issue. This is the strongest position the partner has taken with respect to any deviation. Unlike the basket conversion (which the client will concede), the survival-period reduction is non-negotiable. The client is not willing to entertain any shortening of the survival period for core representations. If the counterparty presses this change, the position is to walk away from the transaction rather than accept the compromise.

D. Recommendation

• Reject any reduction in the survival period for core representations.
• Maintain the survival matrix set forth in Exhibit B as the operative baseline.
• If the counterparty refuses to withdraw the shortened limitation period, treat this as a walk-away issue consistent with the controlling partner instruction.
• No concession may be offered on this point. The report should reflect that the client's position is firm and the survival-period reduction is a deal-breaker.

---

VI. RECONCILIATION MATRIX

The following table summarizes each deviation, its source, the transfer impact, the controlling partner position, and the recommended response.

Deviation | Source (Counterparty Markup) | Transfer Impact (Schedules/Exhibits) | Controlling Partner Instruction | Recommended Response
---------|------------------------------|-------------------------------------|--------------------------------|----------------------
1. Indemnification cap reduction | Silent cap reduction | Schedule 5.2 — retained liabilities would be silently shifted | Basket conversion conceded; cap reduction not addressed | Accept basket conversion; reject cap reduction
2. Basket conversion (deductible → tipping) | Silent conversion | Schedule 5.2 — interaction with retained liabilities | Client will concede the basket conversion | Accept
3. MAE definition carve-outs for regulatory action | New carve-outs for regulatory action of the kind at issue | Schedule 3.7 — two pending regulatory inquiries directly intersect | No specific instruction; substantive risk allocation issue | Reject carve-outs; narrow if necessary; escalate
4. Limitation period shortening survival | New limitation period | Exhibit B — contradicts survival matrix | Any survival-period reduction is a walk-away issue | Reject; walk away if not withdrawn

---

VII. ADDITIONAL OBSERVATIONS

1. The counterparty's markup is predominantly consistent with the firm-standard playbook; only the three deviations identified above depart from the base materials.

2. The Schedule 3.7 disclosures are critical to the MAE analysis. The two pending regulatory inquiries constitute known risks that the counterparty is attempting to carve out of the agreement's risk-allocation framework. This is not a market-standard carve-out and should be resisted.

3. The combined effect of the indemnification cap reduction and basket conversion, when read against Schedule 5.2, creates ambiguity regarding which party bears which retained liabilities. This must be clarified before any concession is finalized.

4. Exhibit B provides the operative survival matrix. Any deviation from the Exhibit B survival periods, including the counterparty's proposed limitation-period change, must be treated in accordance with the partner's controlling instruction.

5. All recommendations in this report reflect the latest partner instruction. Any prior email or correspondence stating contradictory priorities is superseded and does not govern.

---

VIII. CONCLUSION

The counterparty's markup introduces three material deviations from the original draft, each of which has been assessed against the transfer impact summary and the controlling partner instructions. The client will accept the basket conversion. The indemnification cap reduction should be rejected absent further authorization. The MAE carve-outs for regulatory action should be rejected because they are designed to neutralize the two pending regulatory inquiries disclosed on Schedule 3.7. Critically, the shortening of the survival period for core representations is a walk-away issue: the client will not accept any reduction, and the survival matrix in Exhibit B must be maintained. The recommended responses set forth above should guide the next round of negotiations.

END OF REPORT
